newsitem.title: ITALY: Kenya chides U.N. over Zaire intervention force.
newsitem.headline: Kenya chides U.N. over Zaire intervention force.

text.p: Kenya, which this month hosted a summit on the refugee crisis in eastern Zaire, chided the United Nations on Thursday for failing to discuss an international intervention force with African nations.

President Daniel arap Moi told a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit that his country was "surprised to learn through the media, and without consultation with us, that there is to be international intervention in the region."

"The Nairobi summit passed resolutions which among others called for the respect of the territorial integrity of Zaire and a plea for humanitarian support for the victims of this conflict," Moi said in his speech to the summit.
He said the resolutions passed were clear and the United Nations Security Council had endorsed them.

"My colleagues and I expected the United Nations to consult with us through the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) before embarking on any action directed at the solution of the crisis," Moi added.

The Kenyan leader said that the Nairobi summit on November 5 had put forward "practical ideas on how to handle the situation to avoid a Somali-like intervention which was too expensive in terms of human and material cost".

The U.N. Security Council was preparing to vote later on Friday on a resolution to send a multinational force to ease the plight of an estimated 1.2 million Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi scattered across war-ravaged eastern Zaire.
Hundreds of thousands of them began heading home on Friday in a trek that could signal a breakthrough in humanitarian attempts to keep them from starving to death.
Moi said the crisis was senseless and added that the scenes of agony from Zaire broadcast on television around the world should "prick the consciences of all people".
The United States has agreed to commit troops to the Canadian-led multinational force due to be deployed within days.
Diplomats have said the initial force is expected to be made up of troops from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal.
Moi said that guaranteeing peace and stability in the region was "part and parcel" of food security efforts.
"Failure to achieve peace will create unstable conditions which escalate food insecurity," he warned.
